title: A journalist finds a new beat: His imprisonment
text:
A journalist finds a new beat: His imprisonment
In early 2023, Evan Gershkovich was leading a charmed life. The son of Russian émigrés who moved to New Jersey before he was born, he was a Moscow-based foreign correspondent for The Wall Street Journal. He spoke Russian fluently and had a large group of friends. The war between Russia and Ukraine was underway, so he had plenty of stories to cover and the freedom to follow them.
But in March of that year, Gershkovich met a source to discuss a story about Russian tank production. Shortly after they began to talk, Russian security forces burst through the door and arrested him for espionage.
He tells the story of his arrest, imprisonment, trial, and eventual release in “This Cursed Beautiful Land: A Russian-American Story.” What makes his tale unique is that it is so carefully reported with nuance, colorful and vivid descriptions, and even humor.
When a Wall Street Journal reporter was arrested in Russia, he began taking notes during the politically motivated ordeal. His memoir is a tale of resilience.
After his arrest, he was confined to Lefortovo prison and realized that he was an unwilling participant in “hostage diplomacy” – the practice of detaining citizens of another country as a political bargaining chip. Given his circumstances, he decided to spend his time reporting on what happened to him while he was locked up.
“Well, there’s nothing much I can do,” he told himself. “I’m here, I can’t get out of here and, honestly, it’s interesting. I’m a reporter, after all.”
In short, he made the Russian prison system his “beat.”
The assignment would last for 491 days.
By the time of his arrest, Lefortovo had been transformed into what passed for, in Russia, a model prison. Gershkovich was not subject to beatings, solitary confinement, or torture. He received regular exercise and the food was satisfactory, if not plentiful.
He got along well with his cellmate, who educated him on the many informal rules that govern prison life. So, he learned to wipe his feet on the rug before entering a cell, how to shake hands with another inmate, and the proper etiquette for using the cell’s toilet. He even learned to cook using the small electric kettle in the cell. The two men quickly developed a close friendship and relied on each other for emotional support.
Life was organized around daily rituals. The men carefully cleaned their cell every morning. Care packages and mail arrived on Wednesdays. Gershkovich’s court-appointed lawyers – who were kind and supportive – visited every Thursday. Watching soccer on the television was the major priority on Saturday and Sunday.
He also knew that he was treated well compared with other prisoners because he was a bargaining chip and therefore had to be kept “in pristine shape.”
Even so, he found more humanity and kindness than he expected, and his descriptions are often recounted with warmth and humor. That doesn’t mean he wasn’t frustrated, unhappy, and anxious to get out. Yet rarely does he report feelings of anger, despondency, or hopelessness.
Constant rumors of an impending prisoner swap also provided some comfort. Everyone – other prisoners, guards, his attorneys, the U.S. Embassy staff, even his family in the United States – told him that “a deal is in the works.” But every promising report faded away.
Suddenly, things changed. The Security Service formally accused him of espionage. The evidence was embarrassingly thin, but he was quickly tried, hastily convicted, and sentenced to 16 years in a penal colony. The process was sped up because a complex deal for a large swap of prisoners finally came together: 16 people were released from Russian custody and eight were freed from five Western countries. For form’s sake, the Russians felt they had to convict him before they could release him.
Gershkovich had a joyful return to the United States and reunion with his family and girlfriend. But the hardest part of the ordeal was still before him. The emotions he suppressed while in prison surfaced. Gershkovich became irritable. Crying frequently and unexpectedly, he had trouble sleeping and making decisions. He froze in crowds, and was overwhelmed by human contact. Ironically, once he was free, he felt he had no sense of control.
Over time, Gershkovich regained his emotional balance and began to sort out his feelings. He did not emerge from his ordeal hating Russia or the Russians. Indeed, on the way to the airport and freedom, he wondered longingly whether he would ever see Russia again. If anything, the experience appears to have increased his affection for the Russian people, while it deepened his appreciation of how the country’s long history of brutal authoritarianism continues to trap them.
Most impressive, perhaps, is the dignity, self-control, and calm that Gershkovich demonstrated while facing unimaginable trials and without much of a support network. Most readers will hope that, if faced with the same challenges, they would exhibit similar levels of courage and grace.
